sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: Displaced by the Huns, Gothic groups moved toward the Roman frontier. The Tervingi were admitted into the empire in 376, and the Greuthungi crossed without permission. Relations with Roman officials broke down and the Goths revolted.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Valens, emperor in the East, had been campaigning in Syria and returned to deal with the revolt. His nephew Gratian, emperor in the West, had just defeated the Lentienses and was marching east to join him.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Ammianus says Valens, envious of Gratian's success and urged on by courtiers, wanted a victory of his own before his nephew arrived. Fritigern sought land in Thrace for his people and, in Ammianus's account, negotiated partly to gain time for his cavalry to return.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: Livius places the battle about 13 km north of Adrianople (modern Edirne), near the village of Büyükdöllük. The Goths' wagons formed a ring on rising ground. It was a hot August day, and the Goths set fires to dry the plain.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Valens led his elite eastern troops, including veterans. Fritigern commanded the Tervingi, with Greuthungi under Alatheus and Saphrax, Alans and others. Ammianus says the scouts reported a far smaller Gothic force than was actually nearby, because the cavalry was away. Army sizes are not repeated here.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Valens fortified a camp near the city and held a council at which Sebastianus urged an attack and Victor urged waiting for Gratian. Valens marched out, leaving his baggage and treasury at Adrianople, and reached the Gothic wagon circle around the eighth hour. The right-wing cavalry deployed first while the rest of the column was still coming up.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: Negotiations were still under way, with Richomeres volunteering as a hostage, when archers and light troops under Bacurius and Cassio attacked too early and fell back. The Gothic cavalry under Alatheus and Saphrax then returned and struck. The Roman left advanced almost to the wagons but, unsupported, was overwhelmed; the infantry was pressed so close together that it could hardly fight, and the line broke in dust and confusion.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Valens's decision to attack without waiting for Gratian, on a faulty scouting report and after a long march in the heat, is the central choice. Fritigern's negotiations, in Ammianus's view, bought time for the Gothic cavalry.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The return of the Gothic cavalry against a Roman army only partly deployed decided the battle.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: Valens was killed and his body was never found; Ammianus gives two versions of his death. Many senior officers fell, and Ammianus compares the disaster with Cannae.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: A large part of the eastern field army and many experienced officers were lost. Valens's successor Theodosius made peace with the Goths by 382; Livius says he had to grant land to the victors, while Britannica says the Romans first drove the Goths back to Thrace.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Faulty intelligence, impatience and a tired, thirsty army deployed piecemeal against an enemy whose full strength was not yet in view. Waiting for the army to concentrate might have changed the outcome.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Ammianus treated the battle as a turning point; Livius says many later writers followed him although the view is not necessarily correct, while Britannica presents it as a victory of horsemen over elite infantry and the start of serious Germanic inroads. Livius's pages give two dates for Valens's death, 9 and 2 August. The circumstances of his death are uncertain, and Ammianus's figures for Roman losses are not repeated.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Ammianus Marcellinus 31.12–13 is the main narrative. Livius and Britannica, read in a browser, give modern summaries. Orosius was not read.

sources.title: Jordanes: The Battle of Châlons, 451 CE (Getica 38)
The battle of the Catalaunian Plains

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: The Huns under Attila raided the Balkans from 440. In 447 Attila invaded the eastern empire's Balkan provinces, and Theodosius II raised his payments to him. Attila then turned west.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: In 451 the Huns crossed the Rhine, invaded Gaul and sacked Metz. Aetius, the leading Western Roman general, formed a coalition with the Visigothic king Theodoric and other peoples settled in Gaul.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Attila sought plunder and power in Gaul. Aetius needed to protect Gaul without breaking a coalition whose members had their own interests.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The site is unknown. The battle is variously called the Catalaunian Fields, the Campus Mauriacus or Châlons, and scholars place it north, east or west of Troyes. Jordanes describes a plain rising by a sharp slope to a ridge that both armies tried to take.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Aetius's coalition included Romans, Visigoths, Alans, Franks, Burgundians, Saxons and others. Attila's army included Ostrogoths, Gepids and other subject peoples under their own kings. Jordanes's figures for Attila's army and for the dead are not credible and are not repeated.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Jordanes places Theodoric and the Visigoths on the right, Aetius and the Romans on the left, and Attila with his best troops in the centre, with the subject peoples on the wings.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: Attila was besieging Orléans when the coalition approached, and he withdrew, probably toward Troyes. In the battle both sides raced for the ridge; Thorismund, Theodoric's son, and Aetius reached it first and threw back the Huns. Dahm describes fighting from mid-afternoon into the night. Theodoric was killed, and the Visigoths pressed on almost to Attila, who withdrew into his wagon laager. Fighting in the dark was confused.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Taking the ridge first was the coalition's decisive tactical choice. Afterwards the allies chose to besiege Attila's laager rather than storm it, and, Jordanes says, quarrels between Romans and Goths let Attila escape.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The loss of the ridge and the Visigothic advance after Theodoric's death forced Attila onto the defensive behind his wagons.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: Next morning the Huns stayed in their laager. Jordanes says Attila had a pyre of saddles built, meaning to throw himself on it rather than be captured. Attila then withdrew from Gaul.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: Attila invaded Italy in 452, sacking Aquileia and other northern cities before returning home; Livius's timeline says Pope Leo persuaded him to go. Attila died in 453, and Aetius was assassinated in 454.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Coalition armies can win battles but struggle to finish them: once the immediate danger had passed, the allies' separate interests limited the pursuit. Dahm notes that the fighting was mainly a cavalry struggle for a ridge, not a clash on an open plain.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Jordanes wrote about a century later from a Gothic perspective; he drew on the eyewitness Priscus but goes beyond him, and his account, the fullest that survives, differs from others. The location and exact date are uncertain; Dahm gives 20 June. Dahm questions the traditional view of the battle as one of the most decisive in Western history, since Attila remained a threat. Why Aetius let Attila withdraw is not resolved by the sources read here.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Jordanes's Getica 38, in an older translation on the Internet Medieval Sourcebook, is the main narrative. Murray Dahm's article for Osprey Publishing summarizes the modern debates, and Livius's articles supply the wider chronology. Hydatius's chronicle and the rest of the Getica were not read.
